body.hook: In a famous 1950s experiment, people agreed that a short line was longer than it obviously was, just because everyone else in the room said so. How much of what we do is really our own choice?

vocabulary.definition: How other people affect our thoughts, feelings and behaviour.
Changing behaviour or beliefs to match a group.
Following orders from an authority figure.
The tendency to be less likely to help when others are present.
Feeling less responsible when others could act.
When a group's desire for agreement leads to poor decisions.

study.title: The Power of the Group
study.question: How do other people influence what we do?
study.passage:
Study 1, Asch's conformity experiment (1951): Participants judged which of three lines matched a target line. Confederates (actors) gave obviously wrong answers. About 75% of participants conformed at least once; overall about one third of answers conformed. Conformity dropped sharply when even one other person gave the right answer.
Study 2, Milgram's obedience experiment (1963): Participants were told to give increasing "electric shocks" to a learner (an actor; no real shocks) for wrong answers. About 65% continued to the maximum 450 volts when the experimenter said "Please continue." Obedience dropped when the authority was absent or a peer refused. Ethics: participants experienced serious stress and were deceived; today's ethics rules would not allow it in this form.
Study 3, Bystander effect (Darley and Latané, 1968): Participants who believed others could hear a person having a seizure were less likely and slower to help. Diffusion of responsibility explains it.
Factors that increase conformity and obedience: group size (up to about 4–5), unanimity, authority's status and closeness, uncertainty, culture.
Task: Apply these ideas to three scenarios: a group chat pressuring someone, a supervisor ordering an unsafe shortcut, and a crowd watching someone fall.

study.product: Write a 400-word analysis applying conformity, obedience and the bystander effect to a real or realistic situation, with one strategy to resist harmful influence.

examples.title: Asch
examples.problem: What reduced conformity in Asch's study?
examples.answer: One person giving the correct answer

examples.title: Bystander
examples.problem: Why might no one help someone who falls in a busy mall?
examples.answer: Each person assumes someone else will help

examples.title: Strategy
examples.problem: How can you overcome the bystander effect?
examples.answer: Point to a specific person and give a direct task: "You in the red jacket, call 911"

items.q: Define obedience.
items.answer: Following orders from an authority figure.

items.q: What is conformity?
items.answer: Changing behaviour or beliefs to match a group.

items.q: Summarize Asch's study and its finding.
items.answer: People often conformed to obviously wrong group answers.

items.q: Summarize Milgram's study and its finding.
items.answer: Most participants obeyed orders to give what they thought were strong shocks.

items.q: Explain the bystander effect and its cause.
items.answer: People help less in groups because of diffusion of responsibility.

items.q: Name two factors that increase obedience.
items.answer: Close, high-status authority; legitimate setting; no peers refusing.

items.q: Evaluate the ethics of Milgram's study.
items.answer: Answers vary; deception and stress versus important findings.

items.q: Apply conformity or the bystander effect to a real situation and suggest a strategy.
items.answer: Answers vary.
